name: First Principles Thinking
shortDesc: Break problems to fundamental truths; rebuild from ground up
fullDesc: Strip away assumptions to reach bedrock facts, then reconstruct solutions from scratch. Elon Musk used it to reimagine rockets and batteries. Most powerful when inherited constraints feel immovable.
howToApply: List every assumption. Ask: what is provably true? Discard convention. Rebuild only from verified fundamentals.
whenToUse: Existing solutions seem too costly or slow
Industry norms feel like immovable constraints
You need a breakthrough, not an incremental fix
commonMistakes: Stopping at the first reasoning layer instead of going deeper
Confusing widely-held beliefs with fundamental truths

name: Second-Order Thinking
shortDesc: Consider consequences of consequences, not just immediate effects
fullDesc: First-order thinking stops at the obvious result. Second-order asks: and then what? Separates sophisticated thinkers from the crowd by anticipating downstream effects before acting.
howToApply: After identifying the first consequence, ask 'and then what?' at least twice more. Map the chain before committing.
whenToUse: Any decision affecting many people over time
commonMistakes: Stopping at one level of consequences
Treating second-order effects as too uncertain to consider

name: Inversion
shortDesc: Solve by thinking about what to avoid, then don't do it
fullDesc: Instead of asking how to succeed, ask how to guarantee failure — then avoid those things. Charlie Munger credits inversion as one of his most useful thinking tools for avoiding mistakes.
howToApply: Define your goal. Ask: what would guarantee I fail? List those. Treat them as hard constraints to avoid.
whenToUse: Evaluating a plan for hidden flaws
Trying to understand why past attempts failed
commonMistakes: Only inverting once without exploring multiple failure paths
Inverting but then not acting on the insights

name: Eisenhower Matrix
shortDesc: Sort tasks by urgent/important into four quadrants
fullDesc: Four quadrants: Do (urgent+important), Schedule (important, not urgent), Delegate (urgent, not important), Delete (neither). Forces you to distinguish busyness from actual importance.
howToApply: List all pending tasks. Assign each to a quadrant. Protect time for Quadrant 2 (important, not urgent) — it's where strategy lives.
whenToUse: Deciding what to delegate or drop
commonMistakes: Spending all time in Q1 firefighting and ignoring Q2
Mislabeling urgent tasks as important

name: 80/20 Rule (Pareto Principle)
shortDesc: 80% of results come from 20% of causes
fullDesc: A robust empirical pattern: a minority of inputs drive the majority of outputs. Applies to revenue (20% of customers = 80% of sales), bugs, relationships, and time spent.
howToApply: Identify your top outputs. Trace back which inputs produced them. Double down on those 20% and ruthlessly reduce the rest.
commonMistakes: Treating 80/20 as exact (it's a heuristic)
Cutting the 80% without checking dependencies

name: 5 Whys
shortDesc: Ask why five times to reach root cause
fullDesc: Iterative interrogation technique that drills through symptom layers to find true root cause. Prevents treating symptoms instead of underlying problems. Five is a guide, not a rule — sometimes fewer, sometimes more.
howToApply: State the problem. Ask why it happened. Take that answer and ask why again. Repeat until you reach a cause you can actually fix.
whenToUse: Any time a fix has failed more than once
commonMistakes: Stopping at the first plausible cause
Blaming people rather than systems

name: Occam's Razor
shortDesc: Prefer the simplest explanation that fits the evidence
fullDesc: Among competing explanations, favour the one requiring the fewest assumptions. Not a rule that simple is always right, but a prior: complexity needs justification.
howToApply: List competing explanations. Count assumptions each requires. Default to the simplest unless evidence specifically forces a more complex one.
commonMistakes: Using it to dismiss complex-but-true explanations
Conflating simple with simplistic

name: Hanlon's Razor
shortDesc: Never attribute to malice what can be explained by incompetence
fullDesc: Default to incompetence or oversight before assuming ill intent. Reduces conflict escalation and allows more accurate diagnosis of problems. Especially useful in organisations.
howToApply: Before concluding someone acted maliciously, list plausible non-malicious explanations. Only assign malice if those explanations fail.
commonMistakes: Using it to excuse genuinely harmful patterns
Applying it so broadly you miss real bad actors

name: Goodhart's Law
shortDesc: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
fullDesc: Any metric used as a performance target gets gamed, deliberately or not. The measure loses its validity. Happens in schools, companies, governments — everywhere metrics are tied to incentives.
howToApply: For any metric you track, ask: what behaviour does optimising this incentivise? Check for gaming. Use multiple complementary measures rather than one target.
commonMistakes: Assuming metrics are neutral
Replacing a gamed metric with another single metric that will also get gamed

name: Feedback Loops
shortDesc: Outputs that become inputs, either amplifying or stabilising the system
fullDesc: Reinforcing loops amplify change (compound interest, viral growth). Balancing loops resist change (thermostat, body temperature). Understanding which type dominates predicts system behaviour.
howToApply: Map the key variables in your system. Draw arrows showing how each influences others. Label loops R (reinforcing) or B (balancing). Identify dominant loops.
whenToUse: Understanding why a trend accelerates or slows
Diagnosing why interventions have unintended effects
commonMistakes: Treating all feedback as negative (balancing)
Ignoring time delays between cause and effect

name: Map Is Not the Territory
shortDesc: Our models of reality are not reality itself — beware mistaking them
fullDesc: Every model, plan, or mental representation is a simplification. The danger is acting as if the map is complete. Markets crash, plans fail — often because someone trusted their model more than reality.
howToApply: For any model or plan you rely on, explicitly list what it omits or assumes. Seek data from reality, not just your model of it.
whenToUse: When a model keeps predicting wrong
Interpreting any data visualisation or report
commonMistakes: Updating the map when reality disagrees instead of updating your beliefs
Assuming missing data means the modelled world is complete

name: Leverage Points
shortDesc: Places in a system where a small shift produces big changes
fullDesc: Meadows identified 12 places to intervene in a system, ranked from low to high leverage. The highest leverage — changing the goals or paradigm of the system — are hardest to see and most resisted.
howToApply: Map your system. Identify where small changes have historically produced large effects. Prioritise intervening at the rules/goals level over the numbers level.
whenToUse: Diagnosing why improvement efforts aren't working
Choosing where to invest limited reform energy
commonMistakes: Intervening at low-leverage points (budgets, numbers) while ignoring structure
Underestimating resistance to high-leverage changes

name: Availability Heuristic
shortDesc: Judge probability by how easily examples come to mind
fullDesc: We treat vivid, recent, or dramatic events as more probable than statistics justify. Plane crashes feel more dangerous than car trips. Media coverage distorts perceived risk.
howToApply: When estimating probability, pause and ask: am I overweighting this because it's memorable? Look up actual base rates before concluding.
whenToUse: Policy decisions influenced by recent events
commonMistakes: Conflating ease of recall with actual frequency
Not correcting even after recognising the bias

name: Confirmation Bias
shortDesc: Seek, favour, and recall information that confirms existing beliefs
fullDesc: The most pervasive cognitive bias. We notice supporting evidence, dismiss contradictory evidence, and remember what confirms what we already believe. Infects research, investing, and relationships equally.
howToApply: For any belief you hold strongly, actively search for the best evidence against it. Ask: what would change my mind? If nothing could, that's a warning sign.
whenToUse: Evaluating a hypothesis or business case
Any time you feel very certain about something
commonMistakes: Thinking awareness of the bias is enough to prevent it
Only seeking disconfirming evidence from weak sources

name: Survivorship Bias
shortDesc: Focus on successes while ignoring unseen failures
fullDesc: We study winners because they're visible; losers disappear. WWII engineers studied returning planes for where to add armour — Wald realised the holes showed where planes could survive hits, not where they needed protection.
howToApply: For any success story you're drawing lessons from, ask: where is the graveyard of similar attempts that failed? What would the failure cases tell us?
whenToUse: Learning from successful companies or people
commonMistakes: Treating visible survivors as a representative sample
Building strategies based only on what worked for visible successes

name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
shortDesc: Continue investing because of past investment, not future value
fullDesc: Past costs are gone regardless of what you do next. Rationally, only future costs and benefits should matter. But we feel compelled to justify past spending, leading to escalating commitment to failing paths.
howToApply: Ask: if I had not already spent X, would I start this project today? If no, past costs are distorting your judgment. Decide based only on future costs vs benefits.
whenToUse: Deciding whether to continue a struggling project
Relationship or career decisions with heavy prior investment
Evaluating whether to cut a losing position
commonMistakes: Confusing sunk costs with valuable learning already captured
Abandoning projects too early using sunk cost as excuse

name: Loss Aversion
shortDesc: Losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains feel good
fullDesc: Losing £100 hurts about twice as much as gaining £100 feels good. Drives risk-averse decisions, poor investing behaviour, and reluctance to cut losses. Hardwired through evolution.
howToApply: When a loss-avoidance instinct drives a decision, reframe: what is the expected value? Would you take this bet if described as a gain scenario instead?
commonMistakes: Treating loss aversion as irrational rather than context-dependent
Ignoring it in high-stakes asymmetric situations

name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
shortDesc: Low-ability individuals overestimate their competence
fullDesc: Novices lack the metacognitive ability to recognise their own gaps. Experts, conversely, tend to underestimate their ability relative to others. Both ends are miscalibrated.
howToApply: Map your confidence against actual feedback and outcomes. Seek experts who will challenge your assessments. Track predictions vs results.
whenToUse: Any high-stakes domain where you are relatively new
commonMistakes: Using it to dismiss confident beginners
Assuming experts are immune (they have their own blind spots)

name: Planning Fallacy
shortDesc: Underestimate time, costs, and risks of future actions
fullDesc: We plan from the inside view — our specific plan — and ignore the outside view (how long similar projects actually take). Almost all projects run over budget and behind schedule.
howToApply: Find reference-class data: how long did similar projects take? Use that as your baseline. Add a deliberate buffer. Plan for known unknowns.
commonMistakes: Adjusting estimates upward slightly rather than referencing base rates
Treating optimistic estimates as motivational targets

name: Dichotomy of Control
shortDesc: Distinguish what is in your control from what isn't; focus on the former
fullDesc: Epictetus divided the world into things 'up to us' (judgments, intentions, desires, actions) and things 'not up to us' (body, reputation, possessions, outcomes). Suffering comes from confusing the two.
howToApply: In any stressful situation, list what you can control and what you cannot. Redirect all energy to the controllable. Mentally release the rest.
whenToUse: Anxiety about outcomes outside your control
commonMistakes: Using it as an excuse for passivity on things you can influence
Incorrectly categorising influence as control

name: Memento Mori
shortDesc: Remember you will die; let mortality clarify what matters
fullDesc: The Stoics kept death front of mind not morbidly but practically — to clarify priorities and stop wasting time on trivialities. What would you do differently if you remembered this might be your last year?
howToApply: Ask: if I had one year left, would I spend today this way? Use mortality as a filter for what truly matters versus what feels urgent but isn't.
whenToUse: Feeling caught in trivial conflicts or status games
commonMistakes: Treating it as morbid rather than clarifying
Using it only in crisis rather than as a regular practice

name: Epistemic Humility
shortDesc: Acknowledge the limits of your own knowledge
fullDesc: The wisest people know how little they know. Epistemic humility means holding beliefs proportional to evidence, being genuinely open to revision, and resisting overconfidence — especially in complex domains.
howToApply: Assign explicit confidence levels to your key beliefs. Maintain a log of predictions with outcomes. Actively notice when you were wrong.
commonMistakes: Performing humility while still anchoring hard to first beliefs
Treating all opinions as equally uncertain regardless of evidence

name: Jobs-to-be-Done
shortDesc: Customers hire products to do a job; understand the job, not the product
fullDesc: People don't buy products — they hire them to make progress in their life. Understanding the functional, emotional, and social job being done reveals what truly drives switching behaviour and loyalty.
howToApply: Interview customers about a recent purchase or switch. Ask what situation prompted it, what they hoped to accomplish, what alternatives they considered.
commonMistakes: Focusing on product attributes rather than the progress customers seek
Conflating the job with the demographic segment

name: Competitive Moats
shortDesc: Durable competitive advantages that protect long-term profitability
fullDesc: Moats include network effects, switching costs, cost advantages, intangible assets (brands/patents), and efficient scale. Without a moat, profits attract competition and erode. With one, they compound.
howToApply: For your business, identify which moat type(s) you have or could build. Ask: why can't a well-funded competitor copy this in 3 years?
whenToUse: Deciding where to invest for defensibility
commonMistakes: Confusing market share with a moat (share can be competed away)
Building only one moat type when multiple are possible

name: Innovator's Dilemma
shortDesc: Successful companies can fail by serving existing customers too well
fullDesc: Incumbents rationally ignore disruptive technologies because they underserve current customers. Meanwhile, disruptors improve until they meet mainstream needs — then the incumbent collapses with no viable response.
howToApply: Map the performance trajectory of emerging alternatives. Ask: if they keep improving at current rate, when do they satisfy our core customers? Plan your response before that.
commonMistakes: Dismissing disruption because it underperforms today
Confusing sustaining innovation with disruptive innovation

name: Correlation vs Causation
shortDesc: Two things moving together does not mean one causes the other
fullDesc: Correlation measures co-movement. Causation requires mechanism, temporal precedence, and ruling out confounders. Ice cream sales and drowning rates correlate — both are caused by summer heat.
howToApply: For any claimed causal relationship, ask: is there a plausible mechanism? Could a third variable explain both? Has this been tested with controlled experiments?
commonMistakes: Accepting plausible-sounding mechanisms as proof of causation
Dismissing all observational evidence as non-causal

name: Black Swan Theory
origin: Nassim Nicholas Taleb · The Black Swan
shortDesc: Rare, high-impact events that are unpredictable but explicable in hindsight
fullDesc: Black swans have three properties: extreme rarity, severe impact, and retrospective (not prospective) predictability. Most historic turning points were black swans. Preparing for them differs from predicting them.
howToApply: Build robustness and optionality rather than optimising for the expected scenario. Avoid situations with catastrophic downside even if they seem low probability.
commonMistakes: Treating all tail risks as black swans (some are foreseeable)
Conflating improbable with impossible

name: Scientific Method
origin: Francis Bacon · The Advancement of Learning
shortDesc: Hypothesise, test, measure, revise — the engine of reliable knowledge
fullDesc: The most reliable knowledge-building process humans have: observe, form hypothesis, design experiment to falsify it, measure, update. Requires willingness to be wrong and mechanisms to catch errors.
howToApply: State your hypothesis explicitly. Design the minimum test that would disprove it. Run the test. Update your belief based on the result, not your prior.
whenToUse: Testing business assumptions before full commitment
Any claim that needs to be more than opinion
commonMistakes: Designing experiments that can only confirm, not falsify
Updating beliefs insufficiently after disconfirming results

name: Fermi Estimation
shortDesc: Break down unknown quantities into estimable components
fullDesc: Fermi could estimate the number of piano tuners in Chicago from first principles. By chaining reasonable estimates for each component, you get an answer within an order of magnitude — often good enough to act on.
howToApply: Decompose the unknown quantity into components you can estimate. Estimate each. Multiply or sum. Sanity check against anything you can verify.
whenToUse: Quick viability checks before deep research
commonMistakes: Compounding optimistic estimates in each step
Treating the result as precise rather than a rough range

name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
origin: Abraham Maslow · A Theory of Human Motivation
shortDesc: Physiological→Safety→Love→Esteem→Self-actualisation — lower needs first
fullDesc: Maslow proposed that human needs form a hierarchy: only when lower-level needs are met can higher-level ones motivate behaviour. Broadly applicable in product design, management, and understanding stakeholder behaviour.
howToApply: Identify which need level is unmet for your audience or team. You cannot motivate with esteem rewards if safety needs feel threatened.
commonMistakes: Treating the hierarchy as strictly sequential (needs overlap in practice)
Assuming self-actualisation is the only 'real' motivation

name: Growth vs Fixed Mindset
shortDesc: Growth: abilities develop through effort. Fixed: abilities are innate
fullDesc: People with a growth mindset see challenges as opportunities to develop; those with a fixed mindset see them as tests of fixed ability. Mindset predicts resilience, learning speed, and response to failure.
howToApply: Notice your self-talk when you fail or struggle. 'I'm not good at this' is fixed; 'I'm not good at this yet' is growth. Deliberately seek challenges at the edge of your ability.
commonMistakes: Praising effort regardless of strategy (effort without learning is just activity)
Thinking mindset is binary — it's domain-specific and situational

name: Flow State
shortDesc: Deep concentration and effortless engagement when challenge meets skill
fullDesc: Flow is the optimal experience of total absorption. It occurs when challenge level matches skill level. Too easy produces boredom; too hard produces anxiety. The channel between them is flow.
howToApply: Identify your current skill level in a domain. Choose tasks slightly above it. Eliminate interruptions. Set clear immediate goals. Review what conditions produced your best flow experiences.
commonMistakes: Mistaking busy-ness for flow
Ignoring environmental conditions that block flow (notifications, ambiguous goals)

name: Cognitive Dissonance
origin: Leon Festinger · A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance
shortDesc: Discomfort from holding contradictory beliefs; we resolve it by rationalising
fullDesc: When our beliefs or actions conflict, we feel psychological discomfort. We resolve it — usually by changing beliefs to fit actions rather than changing actions. Understanding this explains irrational loyalty and post-hoc rationalisation.
howToApply: Notice when you feel discomfort after a decision. Ask: am I rationalising rather than reasoning? Check if your updated belief would have led you to the same decision in advance.
commonMistakes: Assuming it only affects others
Using it as an excuse to keep irrational beliefs unchanged

name: Opportunity Cost
shortDesc: Every choice has a cost — the value of the best alternative foregone
fullDesc: The true cost of any decision includes what you give up. Spending £1M on marketing means not spending it on product. Time at meeting A means not working on project B. Invisible costs are still real.
howToApply: Before any significant resource allocation, explicitly identify the best alternative use. Compare the expected return of both before committing.
whenToUse: Evaluating whether to stay in a role or pursue an opportunity
commonMistakes: Only considering explicit costs, not foregone alternatives
Paralysis from identifying too many alternatives — just the best one matters

name: Nudge Theory
shortDesc: Shape choices by changing default options and the choice architecture
fullDesc: People take the path of least resistance. By changing what the default is, you change what most people do — without restricting freedom. Opt-out organ donation increases donors dramatically over opt-in.
howToApply: Identify the behaviour you want to encourage. Make it the default, the easiest option, or the most visible one. Reduce friction for desired behaviour; add friction for undesired.
commonMistakes: Using nudges to manipulate rather than help users achieve their own goals
Ignoring that defaults carry an implicit ethical endorsement

name: Servant Leadership
origin: Robert K. Greenleaf · The Servant as Leader
shortDesc: Leaders exist to serve their team, removing obstacles and growing people
fullDesc: Inverts the traditional hierarchy: leaders exist for their team, not the other way around. The servant-leader's job is to remove blockers, develop people, and create conditions for excellent work.
howToApply: Ask your team weekly: what is blocking you? Make resolving those blockers your priority. Measure your effectiveness by your team's growth and output, not your own visibility.
commonMistakes: Treating every request as a command (it can become people-pleasing)
Neglecting direction-setting — servants still need to know where they're going

name: Psychological Safety
shortDesc: Teams perform best when members feel safe to speak up and take risks
fullDesc: Google's Project Aristotle found psychological safety was the top predictor of team performance. It's the shared belief that the team won't punish speaking up, disagreeing, or admitting mistakes.
howToApply: Model vulnerability as a leader — admit uncertainty and mistakes openly. Respond to bad news with curiosity, not blame. Reward problem-raising, not just problem-solving.
whenToUse: Any environment where errors have serious consequences
commonMistakes: Confusing psychological safety with being nice (it requires candour)
Creating safety without accountability — high safety + low standards = mediocrity

name: Radical Candor
shortDesc: Care personally while challenging directly — kind honesty
fullDesc: Two axes: how much you care about the person, and how directly you challenge them. Radical Candor is high on both. Ruinous Empathy (caring but avoiding hard truths) is the most common failure mode.
howToApply: Before giving feedback, confirm you genuinely care about the person's success. Then say the hard thing clearly and specifically — not softened into meaninglessness.
commonMistakes: Mistaking bluntness for candor (challenge must come from genuine care)
Confusing Obnoxious Aggression (challenging without caring) with candor

name: Design Thinking
shortDesc: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test — human-centred problem solving
fullDesc: A non-linear, iterative process for solving complex human problems. Starts with deep empathy to understand the real problem before jumping to solutions. Failing fast in prototype stage is a feature, not a bug.
howToApply: Before ideating solutions, spend disproportionate time with real users. Define the problem as a 'How might we...?' statement. Generate many options before converging. Prototype the riskiest assumption first.
whenToUse: Any problem where user behaviour matters
commonMistakes: Skipping empathy to jump straight to ideation
Treating the stages as strictly sequential — they're meant to overlap

name: Feynman Technique
shortDesc: Explain a concept simply; identify gaps when you can't
fullDesc: True understanding means you can explain something simply. Write out your explanation as if teaching a child. Where you use jargon or get vague, that's exactly your gap. Go back and fill it.
howToApply: Write the concept name. Explain it in plain language without jargon. Where you struggle, return to the source. Simplify further until the explanation is clear and jargon-free.
whenToUse: Checking if you actually understand something or just recognise it
commonMistakes: Stopping when it sounds plausible rather than genuinely simple
Mistaking familiarity with jargon for understanding

name: Spaced Repetition
shortDesc: Review information at increasing intervals to lock it in long-term memory
fullDesc: Memory decays predictably. Reviewing material at increasing intervals (1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 1 month...) exploits the spacing effect to move knowledge from working to long-term memory efficiently.
howToApply: Use an SRS tool (Anki, etc.) or schedule explicit review sessions at increasing intervals. Prioritise active recall over re-reading — test yourself, don't just reread.
whenToUse: Learning languages or large factual bodies of knowledge
commonMistakes: Re-reading instead of active recall
Reviewing too frequently (defeats the purpose of spacing)

name: Aristotle's Rhetorical Triangle
shortDesc: Ethos (credibility), Pathos (emotion), Logos (logic) — the three pillars of persuasion
fullDesc: Effective persuasion uses all three: Ethos (why should they trust you?), Pathos (why should they care emotionally?), Logos (what's the logical argument?). Weaknesses in any pillar weaken the whole case.
howToApply: Before a pitch or presentation, explicitly draft your Ethos, Pathos, and Logos elements. Check you haven't skipped one. Often Pathos is the weakest in technical presentations.
commonMistakes: Relying only on logic for technical audiences
Credibility (Ethos) borrowed from title rather than demonstrated competence

name: Steelmanning
shortDesc: Argue against the strongest version of your opponent's position
fullDesc: The opposite of a strawman. Before disagreeing, construct the best possible version of the other side's argument. This ensures you're engaging with the real disagreement, builds credibility, and often reveals something true in their view.
howToApply: Before responding to a disagreement, articulate their position charitably until they'd say 'yes, that's what I mean.' Only then respond to that version.
whenToUse: Strengthening your own arguments by stress-testing them
commonMistakes: Mistaking the stated position for the real one without probing
Using steelmanning as a rhetorical manoeuvre rather than a genuine commitment

name: Natural Selection
origin: Charles Darwin · On the Origin of Species
shortDesc: Traits that improve survival and reproduction spread through populations
fullDesc: Variation exists in any population; heritable traits that increase reproductive success become more common over generations. Applies as a mental model beyond biology: ideas, companies, and habits also evolve by selection.
howToApply: In any competitive system, ask: what traits lead to survival here? What leads to elimination? Are you optimising for the right selection criteria?
whenToUse: Understanding why institutions or ideas persist
Designing systems that improve over time
commonMistakes: Assuming selection always produces optimal outcomes (it produces locally fit, not globally optimal)
Applying 'survival of the fittest' in contexts with very different selection pressures

name: Identity-Based Habits
shortDesc: Change behaviour by changing self-image first — be, then do
fullDesc: Outcomes-based habits (I want to lose weight) are fragile. Identity-based habits (I am a healthy person) are durable because each action is a vote for the identity you want. The goal is to become the type of person who does the thing.
howToApply: Define the identity you want: 'I am a writer', 'I am someone who exercises.' For each habit you want to build, ask: what would this type of person do? Do that thing.
whenToUse: Breaking old habits that feel automatic
commonMistakes: Jumping to outcomes without anchoring to identity
Identity statements too vague to guide specific action

name: Aggregation of Marginal Gains
shortDesc: 1% improvement in every area compounds to dramatic overall progress
fullDesc: British Cycling's head coach decomposed cycling performance into every component and improved each by 1%. The aggregation produced extraordinary results. Small gains that seem trivial compound into transformational change.
howToApply: List every component contributing to your outcome. Identify the smallest improvement possible in each. Implement systematically. Track compound progress monthly.
whenToUse: When big leaps seem impossible but small steps are feasible
commonMistakes: Optimising isolated components that don't actually compound
Neglecting interactions between components

name: Diffusion of Innovations
shortDesc: Innovations spread through Innovators→Early Adopters→Majority→Laggards
fullDesc: Adoption follows an S-curve. Crossing the chasm between Early Adopters and Early Majority is the critical challenge. Each segment has different motivations and requires different messaging.
howToApply: Identify which segment you're targeting now. Early adopters want to be first; majority want proven solutions. Match your messaging and product positioning to where your target segment sits.
commonMistakes: Treating all potential customers the same way
Not recognising the chasm between early adopters and early majority

name: Social Capital
shortDesc: The value generated by social networks and relationships
fullDesc: Social capital comprises the norms of reciprocity, information channels, and trust embedded in social relationships. High social capital enables coordination, lowers transaction costs, and creates opportunity. It compounds like financial capital.
howToApply: Invest in relationships before you need them. Give value without immediate expectation. Be reliable. Build a diverse network (bridges between clusters have higher value than dense internal clusters).
commonMistakes: Only investing in high-status contacts (weak ties often more valuable)
Treating relationships as transactional — social capital requires genuine reciprocity

name: Lindy Effect
shortDesc: Non-perishable things that have survived long are likely to survive longer
fullDesc: For non-perishable things (ideas, books, technology), every day of survival predicts more future survival. A book that's been in print 100 years will likely be read another 100 years. A 2-year-old startup may not last 2 more.
howToApply: Prioritise learning from ideas, books, and frameworks that have survived decades — they've passed the selection filter of time. Be sceptical of the latest management fad.
whenToUse: Choosing what to study and learn
Evaluating the durability of ideas or institutions
commonMistakes: Applying it to perishable things (Lindy only applies to non-perishables)
Using it to dismiss genuinely new paradigms that make old assumptions obsolete

name: Build-Measure-Learn Loop
shortDesc: Ship fast, measure outcomes, learn and iterate
fullDesc: The core lean startup cycle: build the minimum to test the riskiest assumption, measure what actually happens, learn whether your hypothesis was right, and decide to persist or pivot. Speed through the loop beats perfection.
howToApply: Identify your riskiest assumption. Build the minimum to test it. Define what measurement would falsify it before you build. Run the test. Act on the result.
whenToUse: Any investment of significant time/money before validation
commonMistakes: Building more than needed to test the hypothesis
Measuring vanity metrics instead of behaviour-changing evidence

name: Regret Minimisation Framework
shortDesc: Project to age 80; choose the path you'd regret not taking
fullDesc: Bezos used this to leave Wall Street and start Amazon. Project yourself to age 80 looking back. Which choice would you regret more? Removes short-term emotional noise and surfaces long-term values.
howToApply: Visualise yourself at 80, looking back at today's decision. Would you regret inaction more than action, or the reverse? That's your answer.
whenToUse: Whether to attempt something risky but meaningful
Deciding to leave or stay in a situation
commonMistakes: Conflating what you'd regret with what others expect
Using it for reversible decisions (save it for irreversible ones)

name: Expected Value
shortDesc: Probability × magnitude; compare weighted outcomes
fullDesc: Expected value is the probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes. A 10% chance of £1,000 has EV of £100. Good decision-makers maximise EV, not certainty, and accept variance as the cost of high EV.
howToApply: List possible outcomes and their probabilities. Multiply probability × outcome for each. Sum them. Compare alternatives by their expected value, not their most likely outcome.
whenToUse: Repeated decisions where variance averages out
commonMistakes: Ignoring tail risks that have enormous magnitude even if low probability
Applying EV to one-off irreversible decisions where ruin is possible

name: Premortem Analysis
shortDesc: Imagine failure has occurred; work backwards to prevent it
fullDesc: Before a project starts, gather the team and say: it's one year from now and this project has failed. Why? People generate reasons they'd hold back in a forward-looking meeting. Surfaces hidden concerns without blame.
howToApply: At project kickoff, announce: the project has failed. Everyone writes independently why it failed. Share and discuss. Adjust the plan to address the most credible failure causes.
whenToUse: Any decision with high consequence if wrong
commonMistakes: Turning it into a blame session rather than a planning tool
Running it too late when changes are no longer possible

name: Reversible vs Irreversible Decisions
shortDesc: Move fast on reversible; slow and careful on irreversible
fullDesc: Bezos called these Type 1 (one-way door) and Type 2 (two-way door) decisions. Most decisions are reversible and should be made quickly. The few irreversible ones deserve slow, careful analysis.
howToApply: Before any decision, ask: can this be undone easily and cheaply? If yes, decide fast and iterate. If no, slow down, gather more information, and involve more stakeholders.
whenToUse: Evaluating how much analysis a decision deserves
commonMistakes: Treating reversible decisions with irreversible-level caution (slows everything)
Treating irreversible decisions as reversible (catastrophic)

name: 10/10/10 Rule
shortDesc: How will you feel about this decision in 10 mins, 10 months, 10 years?
fullDesc: A quick temporal perspective-taking tool. Decisions that feel urgent often look trivial from 10 months out. Some that feel small become defining choices at 10 years. Separates emotional urgency from actual importance.
howToApply: Ask the three questions. If the 10-minute feeling dominates the 10-year view, you're being driven by emotion. Weight the time horizon appropriate to the decision's reversibility.
commonMistakes: Always defaulting to the longest time horizon (short-term matters for reversible decisions)
Using it to rationalise avoidance

name: Bayesian Reasoning
shortDesc: Update beliefs when new evidence arrives; prior × likelihood
fullDesc: Bayes' theorem describes rational belief updating. Start with a prior (what you believe before evidence). Multiply by likelihood (how probable this evidence is if your belief is true). Get a posterior (updated belief). Repeat with each new piece of evidence.
howToApply: For any belief, state your prior probability explicitly. When new evidence arrives, ask: how likely is this evidence if my belief is true vs. false? Update proportionally.
commonMistakes: Anchoring too hard to a prior and under-updating
Over-updating on single dramatic pieces of evidence

name: OODA Loop
shortDesc: Observe, Orient, Decide, Act — iterate faster than the opposition
fullDesc: Fighter pilot and strategist John Boyd's framework: Observe (gather data), Orient (interpret via mental models and experience), Decide (choose a course), Act. Winning requires cycling faster than your adversary and disrupting their loop.
howToApply: In competitive situations, identify where your loop is slowest. Often it's Orient — updating mental models with new reality. Build faster feedback into your process.
whenToUse: Any rapidly changing environment requiring fast adaptation
commonMistakes: Optimising Act speed at the expense of Orient quality
Treating the loop as sequential when effective practitioners run them in parallel

name: Margin of Safety
shortDesc: Build in buffer between expected and maximum load
fullDesc: Graham's investing principle generalised: never operate at theoretical maximum. Plan for 80% capacity when you need 100%. Buy at a significant discount to intrinsic value. Build bridges rated 4× their expected load.
howToApply: Identify your key constraints and limits. Add a deliberate buffer proportional to uncertainty and consequence of failure. Treat the buffer as non-negotiable.
commonMistakes: Setting the margin too thin when uncertainty is high
Removing the margin as a cost-cutting measure

name: Cynefin Framework
shortDesc: Map situations to: simple, complicated, complex, or chaotic
fullDesc: Four domains requiring different responses: Clear (best practices), Complicated (expert analysis), Complex (probe-sense-respond), Chaotic (act first). Applying the wrong approach to the wrong domain causes predictable failure.
howToApply: Diagnose which domain your situation inhabits. Clear: follow the rules. Complicated: get experts. Complex: run small experiments. Chaotic: stabilise first, analyse later.
whenToUse: Problem-solving in novel or ambiguous situations
commonMistakes: Treating complex problems with complicated-domain tools (analysis without experimentation)
Staying in chaotic mode after the crisis has passed

name: Chesterton's Fence
shortDesc: Understand why something exists before removing it
fullDesc: If you find a fence across a road and don't know why it's there, you have no right to remove it. Only when you understand its purpose can you decide intelligently to remove it. Prevents naive reforms that destroy hidden value.
howToApply: Before eliminating or changing any policy, process, or structure, explicitly state why it was created. If you can't, find out. Only modify it once you understand the original intent.
commonMistakes: Assuming old = inefficient without understanding the context it was built for
Using it as an excuse to never change anything

name: Minimum Viable Decision
shortDesc: Make the smallest decision that lets you learn and iterate
fullDesc: Applied lean thinking to decisions. Instead of deciding everything upfront, identify the smallest commitment that tests the most important assumption. Preserves optionality and generates real data faster than planning.
howToApply: Before making a full commitment, ask: what is the smallest decision I can make to test whether this direction is right? Make that decision first.
whenToUse: Any situation where learning is more valuable than execution speed
commonMistakes: Making decisions so small they don't actually test the core hypothesis
Using MVD as an excuse for permanent indecision

name: Satisficing vs Maximising
shortDesc: Good enough often beats exhaustive search for the perfect option
fullDesc: Maximisers search for the best possible option; satisficers set a threshold and pick the first option that meets it. Research shows satisficers are happier and less regret-prone, despite (or because of) not optimising.
howToApply: For most decisions, define your threshold criteria before you start searching. Stop when you find something that meets the threshold. Reserve maximising for truly high-stakes irreversible choices.
whenToUse: Any repeated decision under time pressure
commonMistakes: Setting threshold too low (produces poor outcomes)
Satisficing on decisions that genuinely deserve maximising

name: Hitchens's Razor
origin: Christopher Hitchens · God Is Not Great
shortDesc: What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence
fullDesc: The burden of proof lies with the person making a claim. If a claim is made without evidence, no evidence is required to dismiss it. Protects against being obliged to disprove unfalsifiable assertions.
howToApply: When encountering a claim, ask: what evidence supports this? If none is offered, you are not obliged to disprove it — the claim can be set aside.
whenToUse: Evaluating claims in debate or media
commonMistakes: Using it to dismiss claims that have evidence you haven't seen yet
Conflating 'no evidence presented' with 'no evidence exists'

name: Brandolini's Law
shortDesc: The energy to refute nonsense is far greater than to produce it
fullDesc: Also called the Bullshit Asymmetry Principle. Producing misinformation is cheap and fast; refuting it rigorously requires time, evidence, and expertise. This asymmetry makes misinformation an effective weapon.
howToApply: Before engaging to refute a claim, ask: is this worth the asymmetric effort? Often a clear label ('this is false') is more effective than a full refutation that lends credibility.
whenToUse: Deciding whether to engage with misinformation
commonMistakes: Engaging with every bad-faith claim, amplifying it in the process
Giving up on all refutation because it's hard

name: Hume's Guillotine
origin: David Hume · A Treatise of Human Nature
shortDesc: You cannot derive 'ought' from 'is' — facts don't imply values
fullDesc: A foundational point in ethical philosophy: no amount of facts about how things are logically entails how things ought to be. Values require value premises, not just empirical ones. Separates descriptive from normative claims.
howToApply: In any argument that moves from facts to moral conclusions, identify where the value premise is. Make it explicit. Evaluate whether you actually accept that value.
whenToUse: Any argument that moves from data to should
commonMistakes: Accepting 'natural = good' arguments without surfacing the hidden value premise
Assuming facts alone can settle ethical disputes

name: Popper's Falsifiability
origin: Karl Popper · The Logic of Scientific Discovery
shortDesc: A claim is scientific only if it can in principle be proven false
fullDesc: Science advances by falsification, not verification. A theory that explains everything explains nothing. Einstein's relativity made specific predictions that could have been wrong — that's what makes it scientific.
howToApply: For any claim, ask: what evidence would prove this wrong? If no possible evidence could, the claim is not scientific — it may still be meaningful, but it's not science.
whenToUse: Distinguishing testable hypotheses from unfalsifiable beliefs
commonMistakes: Treating unfalsifiability as always wrong (it may be true, just not scientific)
Using it to dismiss claims that are hard but not impossible to falsify

name: Cunningham's Law
shortDesc: The best way to get the right answer is to post the wrong one
fullDesc: People are more motivated to correct a wrong answer than to provide a right one. Used deliberately to elicit knowledge from communities, experts, and peers by providing a plausible but incorrect starting point.
howToApply: When you need information and no one is responding, post a plausible wrong answer. The correction instinct is stronger than the volunteering instinct.
whenToUse: Eliciting feedback or knowledge from experts
Getting useful responses when direct questions fail
commonMistakes: Using it maliciously to spread misinformation
Misattributing the principle to the wrong person in a way that undermines credibility

name: Peter Principle
origin: Laurence J. Peter · The Peter Principle
shortDesc: People rise to their level of incompetence
fullDesc: In hierarchies, competent people are promoted until they reach a role they're no longer competent for — then they stay there. Explains why organisations fill with managers who can't manage.
howToApply: When promoting, evaluate for skills required in the new role, not just performance in the current one. Create technical/expert career paths that don't require management promotion.
commonMistakes: Assuming all senior leaders are necessarily incompetent (some are promoted for right reasons)
Failing to apply it to yourself

name: Iceberg Model
shortDesc: Visible events are driven by hidden patterns, structures, and mental models
fullDesc: Events are visible above the waterline. Below: patterns (trends over time), structures (the rules and relationships that produce patterns), and mental models (the beliefs that created those structures). Sustainable change requires working below the waterline.
howToApply: When you see a problematic event, ask: is this part of a recurring pattern? What structures produce that pattern? What beliefs created those structures? Intervene at the lowest level you can reach.
commonMistakes: Fixing events without addressing patterns
Assuming structural change is impossible and settling for event-level fixes

name: Emergence
shortDesc: Complex behaviour arising from simple rules — the whole is more than its parts
fullDesc: Emergent properties cannot be predicted from the parts alone — they arise from interactions. Ant colonies, markets, consciousness, and cities are all emergent. Trying to manage emergent systems by controlling parts fails.
howToApply: Identify which properties of your system are emergent (not reducible to individual components). Design rules and interactions, not outcomes. Trust the process if you've set the right rules.
commonMistakes: Trying to engineer emergent outcomes directly (they can't be commanded)
Ignoring that bad emergent properties also arise from simple rules

name: Tipping Points
shortDesc: Small changes build until a threshold triggers rapid system change
fullDesc: Many systems have non-linear dynamics: small inputs accumulate invisibly until a threshold is crossed, after which the system changes rapidly and often irreversibly. Climate, social norms, market panics, and viral spread all follow this pattern.
howToApply: Identify the critical threshold in your system. Monitor leading indicators, not lagging ones. Once past a tipping point, stabilisation requires much more force than prevention did.
commonMistakes: Assuming linear extrapolation applies to all systems
Acting only after the threshold is crossed, when reversal is costly or impossible

name: Cobra Effect (Perverse Incentives)
shortDesc: Incentives designed to fix problems sometimes make them worse
fullDesc: The British colonial government in India offered bounties for dead cobras to reduce the population. Entrepreneurs bred cobras for the bounty. When the policy ended, cobras were released, worsening the problem. Incentives routinely produce unintended feedback effects.
howToApply: Before implementing any incentive, run a simulation: how would a rational, self-interested actor game this? Design the incentive to make gaming consistent with the intended behaviour.
commonMistakes: Assuming people respond to incentives as intended
Not monitoring for gaming after implementation

name: Flywheel Effect
shortDesc: Consistent effort compounds into unstoppable momentum
fullDesc: Like a massive flywheel, early effort barely moves it. Each push builds on the last. Eventually momentum becomes self-sustaining. Amazon's flywheel: lower costs → lower prices → more customers → more sellers → lower costs. There is no single turning point — just consistent effort.
howToApply: Map the reinforcing loop in your business or project. Identify the first element to push. Make it consistent rather than sporadic. Track momentum indicators, not just outputs.
commonMistakes: Expecting visible momentum too early and stopping
Pushing multiple non-connected flywheels instead of one coherent loop

name: Path Dependency
shortDesc: Past choices constrain future options even when better paths exist
fullDesc: QWERTY, VHS, and Windows succeeded not because they were best but because early adoption created switching costs that locked in suboptimal standards. Past choices create path-dependent lock-in that rational agents can't easily escape.
howToApply: When evaluating options, identify switching costs from incumbent solutions. Factor in not just current merit but transition cost. When designing systems, consider what lock-in you're creating.
commonMistakes: Assuming best technology always wins
Ignoring the switching costs that make alternatives less attractive despite being better

name: Complex Adaptive Systems
shortDesc: Systems of agents that adapt and self-organise in response to environment
fullDesc: Markets, ecosystems, immune systems, and cities are CAS: many agents follow local rules, producing global patterns no agent intended. CAS are robust but unpredictable; they can't be engineered top-down, only cultivated.
howToApply: Identify whether your system has many interacting adaptive agents. If yes, shift from command-and-control to setting boundary conditions and monitoring emergent patterns. Intervene at rules level, not outcome level.
commonMistakes: Applying linear management techniques to CAS
Expecting stability — CAS are inherently dynamic

name: Anchoring Bias
shortDesc: Over-rely on the first piece of information encountered
fullDesc: The first number or fact encountered acts as an anchor that disproportionately influences subsequent judgments. Salary negotiations, product pricing, and legal settlements are all strongly affected by the first figure stated.
howToApply: Make an independent estimate before seeing any anchor. If you must see the anchor, deliberately consider whether it is too high or too low. Set your own anchor first in negotiations.
commonMistakes: Adjusting from the anchor rather than forming an independent estimate
Not recognising irrelevant anchors (e.g., random numbers still bias estimates)

name: Status Quo Bias
shortDesc: Prefer the current state of affairs even when change is beneficial
fullDesc: People systematically prefer keeping things as they are, weighting losses from change more than gains. Explains why people stay in bad jobs, hold losing investments, and resist beneficial policy changes.
howToApply: When you feel resistance to changing something, ask: if I didn't have the current situation and were choosing fresh, would I choose it? If no, the bias may be holding you back.
whenToUse: Evaluating whether to change an existing system
commonMistakes: Using it to justify every change (sometimes the status quo is genuinely best)
Conflating familiarity with optimality

name: Optimism Bias
shortDesc: Overestimate the likelihood of positive events happening to us
fullDesc: People consistently believe they are more likely than average to experience positive events and less likely to experience negative ones. Fuels entrepreneurship but also produces poor risk management and over-confident plans.
howToApply: Apply the outside view: what is the base rate of success for this type of venture? Adjust your personal estimate toward the base rate. Use pre-mortems to surface downside scenarios you've discounted.
commonMistakes: Eliminating all optimism (some positive bias is adaptive and motivating)
Only correcting for pessimism when optimism is the more common distortion

name: Framing Effect
shortDesc: The way information is presented changes the decision made
fullDesc: '90% survival rate' and '10% death rate' describe identical facts but produce different choices. The frame activates different emotional responses. Effective communicators choose frames deliberately; critical thinkers notice frames.
howToApply: For any important communication, test your message in multiple frames. For decisions you receive, reframe them to check whether your preference changes — if it does, the frame is driving your judgment.
commonMistakes: Assuming your chosen frame is neutral
Only using positive frames when negative frames are sometimes more motivating

name: Narrative Fallacy
origin: Nassim Nicholas Taleb · The Black Swan
shortDesc: Impose a coherent story on random events to feel they make sense
fullDesc: Humans are compulsive story-makers. We connect random events into causal narratives retrospectively, creating false sense of predictability. The same history gets told as inevitable in hindsight, even if it was highly contingent.
howToApply: When reading a success or failure narrative, ask: what's the randomness this story omits? What other outcomes were equally possible but didn't occur?
commonMistakes: Dismissing all narratives (some causal stories are true)
Failing to check whether the narrative predicts anything about the future

name: Halo Effect
shortDesc: One positive trait causes us to assume other positive traits
fullDesc: Attractive people are judged as more intelligent. Successful founders are assumed to be good managers. One salient positive (or negative) attribute colours our perception of everything else. Infects hiring, investing, and relationships.
howToApply: When evaluating people or products, disaggregate attributes and evaluate each independently. Use structured evaluation forms to force dimension-by-dimension assessment.
commonMistakes: Assuming the halo is always positive (negative halos are equally powerful)
Using blind evaluation for all decisions, even where holistic judgment adds value

name: IKEA Effect
shortDesc: We value things more when we help create them
fullDesc: People ascribe disproportionate value to things they've partially assembled or contributed to. Explains why DIY projects feel precious, why teams fight for their own solutions, and why customisation increases loyalty.
howToApply: In product design, involve users in co-creation. In management, give teams ownership over how goals are achieved. In negotiations, let the other side help shape the solution.
commonMistakes: Confusing effort with quality — high effort doesn't mean better output
Creating token participation that isn't genuine co-creation

name: Recency Bias
shortDesc: Give undue weight to recent events when predicting the future
fullDesc: After a market crash, investors expect further crashes. After a boom, they expect boom to continue. Recent experience anchors expectations disproportionately, ignoring the longer historical base rate.
howToApply: Extend your reference time horizon. Look at the longest available history for any pattern you're trying to predict. Ask: am I extrapolating a recent trend, or a long-run one?
whenToUse: Performance reviews after an unusually good or bad period
Strategic planning in rapidly changing markets
commonMistakes: Using very long time horizons when structural change has genuinely made them irrelevant
Correcting for recency bias by overcorrecting to the opposite view

name: Blind Spot Bias
shortDesc: Recognise bias in others but not in ourselves
fullDesc: We are better at spotting cognitive biases in others than in ourselves. This meta-bias makes self-correction especially hard — we believe we're more objective than we are precisely when we're least objective.
howToApply: Seek external observers for your own blind spots. Ask trusted advisors to flag when your reasoning seems distorted. Create decision processes with structural safeguards, not just willpower.
commonMistakes: Believing awareness of blind spots eliminates them
Only creating structural safeguards for others, not yourself

name: Categorical Imperative
origin: Immanuel Kant · Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
shortDesc: Act only according to rules you'd will to become universal law
fullDesc: Kant's supreme principle of morality: act only according to rules that you could consistently will everyone to follow. If universalising your action creates a contradiction (everyone lies), the action is wrong.
howToApply: For any action you're considering, ask: what if everyone in this situation did the same thing? If universalisation leads to contradiction or harm, the action is impermissible.
whenToUse: Evaluating whether an exception for yourself is morally justified
commonMistakes: Applying it mechanically without considering context
Confusing what you'd prefer everyone to do with what you could consistently will

name: Utilitarianism
origin: Jeremy Bentham & John Stuart Mill · Ethics
shortDesc: Maximise overall well-being; the greatest good for the greatest number
fullDesc: The right action is the one that produces the most good for the most people. Focuses on outcomes rather than rules. Mill's refinement adds quality of pleasures. Creates tractable ethical calculus but faces objections about minority rights.
howToApply: Identify all parties affected by a decision. Estimate the well-being impact on each. Choose the action that maximises aggregate well-being, giving equal weight to each person.
whenToUse: Trade-off decisions with clear winner and loser
commonMistakes: Justifying harm to minorities by appealing to majority benefit
Treating all pleasures as equally valuable regardless of their nature

name: Veil of Ignorance
origin: John Rawls · A Theory of Justice
shortDesc: Design systems as if you didn't know your place in them
fullDesc: Rawls asks: what rules would you choose for society if you didn't know whether you'd be born rich or poor, healthy or disabled? This 'veil of ignorance' produces principles that are genuinely fair rather than self-serving.
howToApply: Before designing a system or policy, ask: would I agree to this if I didn't know which role I'd occupy? If you wouldn't agree to be on the losing side, reconsider the design.
commonMistakes: Assuming the original position reveals one clear answer — it's a heuristic, not an algorithm
Applying it to decisions where position genuinely matters and deserves consideration

name: Virtue Ethics
shortDesc: Focus on character and becoming a good person, not just good acts
fullDesc: Instead of asking 'what should I do?', virtue ethics asks 'what kind of person should I be?' Virtues (courage, honesty, justice) are excellences of character developed through practice. The virtuous person acts well naturally, not just by following rules.
howToApply: Identify the virtues relevant to your role. Ask not 'what rule applies?' but 'what would a person of excellent character do here?' Use it as a character development framework, not just a decision tool.
commonMistakes: Treating virtue ethics as vague compared to rules-based ethics — it's highly specific in practice
Using it to justify inconsistent behaviour under the guise of situational judgment

name: Amor Fati
shortDesc: Love your fate — embrace everything that happens as necessary
fullDesc: The Stoics accepted fate; Nietzsche went further — love it. Not mere resignation but active embrace of everything that occurs, including suffering. Transforms obstacles into opportunities by refusing to see them as obstacles at all.
howToApply: When something bad happens, ask: how could this be exactly what was needed? Deliberately reframe obstacles as material to work with, not problems to escape.
commonMistakes: Using it as toxic positivity (it requires honest engagement with difficulty, not denial)
Applying it to situations where action to change the circumstance is possible and appropriate

name: Negative Visualisation
shortDesc: Imagine losing what you value to appreciate it and prepare for loss
fullDesc: The Stoics practised imagining bad outcomes in advance — not to dwell on misfortune but to inoculate against it and rekindle appreciation for what they had. The opposite of positive visualisation.
howToApply: Spend a few minutes visualising the loss of something you take for granted: a relationship, your health, your work. Notice the appreciation this generates. Consider what preparation the visualisation reveals you should do.
whenToUse: Reducing hedonic adaptation to good things
commonMistakes: Confusing it with pessimism or catastrophising
Doing it so rarely it has no effect on daily experience

name: Existentialism
shortDesc: We are radically free; we create our own meaning through choices
fullDesc: Existence precedes essence: there is no predetermined human nature or purpose. We are condemned to be free, and meaning comes from the choices we make and commitments we take on. Bad faith is denying this freedom.
howToApply: When you feel trapped or determined by circumstances, identify where genuine choice actually exists. Own the choices you're making implicitly. Create meaning through commitment to projects and values.
whenToUse: Any situation where you feel like a victim of circumstance
commonMistakes: Treating radical freedom as radical isolation — Sartre emphasised the social dimension of freedom
Using existential freedom to justify nihilism or avoiding commitment

name: Porter's Five Forces
shortDesc: Analyse industry attractiveness via rivalry, suppliers, buyers, substitutes, entrants
fullDesc: Five structural forces determine an industry's long-term profit potential: competitive rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of suppliers, bargaining power of buyers. Together they determine how value is distributed.
howToApply: Rate each force (high/medium/low) for your industry. Industries with five weak forces have high profit potential; strong forces erode it. Use this to decide whether to enter and how to position.
commonMistakes: Treating the forces as static when they shift over time
Ignoring complementors — participants who can change force dynamics positively

name: Blue Ocean Strategy
shortDesc: Create uncontested market space rather than competing in existing markets
fullDesc: Red oceans are crowded, competitive, and zero-sum. Blue oceans are new markets where competition is irrelevant because you've created new value. Cirque du Soleil created a blue ocean by combining theatre and circus.
howToApply: Use the Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create grid: what can you eliminate that competitors take for granted? What create that the industry never offered? Find the intersection of differentiation and low cost.
whenToUse: When competing on price or features is eroding margins
commonMistakes: Treating blue ocean as a one-time exercise rather than ongoing innovation
Creating markets that turn out to have no demand

name: Network Effects
shortDesc: A product becomes more valuable as more people use it
fullDesc: Metcalfe's Law: network value scales as the square of users. Direct network effects (phone, social), indirect (platforms), and data network effects each create compounding advantage. Once established, nearly impossible to dislodge.
howToApply: Identify whether your product benefits from direct, indirect, or data network effects. Design for density: help users find and interact with each other. Survive the cold start problem with targeted seeding.
commonMistakes: Assuming network effects are sufficient without a quality product
Ignoring that local network effects can be disrupted even if global ones exist

name: BATNA
shortDesc: Know your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
fullDesc: Your BATNA is what you do if the current negotiation fails. The stronger your BATNA, the more power you have. Knowing the other side's BATNA reveals their reservation price. Never accept a deal worse than your BATNA.
howToApply: Before any negotiation, explicitly define your best alternative. Improve it if possible. Estimate the other side's BATNA. Never reveal your BATNA unless it's stronger than they think.
whenToUse: Any situation requiring agreement between parties
commonMistakes: Entering negotiations without a defined BATNA
Revealing a weak BATNA when the other side may not know it's weak

name: OKRs
shortDesc: Objectives and Key Results — align ambition with measurable outcomes
fullDesc: OKRs separate direction (Objectives: inspiring, qualitative) from measurement (Key Results: specific, quantifiable, time-bound). Cascaded through organisations to align individual and team work to strategic intent.
howToApply: Write 3-5 ambitious Objectives. For each, write 2-4 Key Results that would prove you've achieved it. Set OKRs quarterly. Review weekly. An OKR achieved 70% is often better than one set conservatively and hit 100%.
commonMistakes: Converting OKRs into to-do lists (KRs should be outcomes, not tasks)
Using OKRs for performance management (they're planning tools, not evaluation tools)

name: Theory of Constraints
shortDesc: Every system has one binding constraint; focus improvement there
fullDesc: Any system's throughput is limited by its single weakest link — the constraint. Improving non-constraints wastes effort. The five focusing steps: identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat.
howToApply: Identify the bottleneck in your system (where work queues up). Make it work as efficiently as possible. Ensure everything else feeds it optimally. Only then consider expanding it.
commonMistakes: Optimising non-constraints (feels productive, achieves little)
Failing to find the new constraint after the current one is resolved

name: Ansoff Matrix
shortDesc: Four growth strategies: market penetration, development, product dev, diversification
fullDesc: A 2x2 of existing/new products vs existing/new markets. Market penetration (lowest risk), market development, product development, and diversification (highest risk). Forces explicit conversation about which growth strategy you're pursuing.
howToApply: Map your current growth initiatives to the matrix. Ensure risk level matches your capacity. Most companies should be concentrated in market penetration before moving to riskier quadrants.
commonMistakes: Pursuing diversification before mastering core market penetration
Treating the quadrants as equally accessible regardless of organisational capability

name: Base Rate Fallacy
shortDesc: Ignore statistical base rates in favour of specific case information
fullDesc: When given both statistical base rates and specific case information, people over-weight the specific and ignore the statistical. A positive cancer test seems alarming until you factor in that the disease affects 1 in 1,000.
howToApply: Before interpreting any specific signal, establish the base rate. Apply Bayes' theorem to combine prior probability with the new evidence. Never ignore the prior.
whenToUse: Any probabilistic reasoning with prior information available
commonMistakes: Completely ignoring base rates once a vivid specific case is present
Using base rates alone without updating for relevant specific information

name: Antifragility
shortDesc: Some things benefit from shocks and volatility — build systems that do
fullDesc: Fragile systems break under stress. Robust systems resist it. Antifragile systems improve from it. Evolution, immune systems, and muscle are antifragile. Financial speculation is fragile. The goal is to build the former and avoid the latter.
howToApply: Identify your fragile exposures (concentrated positions, single points of failure). Reduce them. Find your antifragile exposures (skills, optionality, learning from error) and increase them.
commonMistakes: Confusing robust (unharmed by stress) with antifragile (improved by stress)
Seeking randomness without skin in the game or learning mechanisms

name: Regression to the Mean
shortDesc: Extreme events tend to be followed by more average ones
fullDesc: Extreme performances contain a luck component. Tall fathers have tall-but-not-as-tall sons. The best performer this year likely does slightly worse next year. Intervening after extreme events produces apparent causation that is really regression.
howToApply: After an extreme result (good or bad), assume some component is luck and expect a more average result next time — regardless of any action taken. Evaluate interventions over many trials, not just after extremes.
commonMistakes: Attributing improvements after bad events entirely to your intervention
Not recognising that praising exceptional performance and criticising poor performance both appear to 'work' due to regression

name: Nash Equilibrium
shortDesc: A stable state where no player benefits from changing strategy unilaterally
fullDesc: In any strategic interaction, a Nash Equilibrium is a combination of strategies where no player can improve their outcome by changing their strategy alone. It may not be optimal for all players collectively — that's its tragedy.
howToApply: Map the strategic choices and payoffs for each player. Find the combination where neither player wants to deviate. Use this to predict stable outcomes and identify whether cooperation agreements are self-enforcing.
commonMistakes: Assuming equilibria are optimal or desirable (they're just stable)
Ignoring that multiple equilibria may exist and the path matters

name: Prisoner's Dilemma
shortDesc: Two rational actors may fail to cooperate even when cooperation is optimal
fullDesc: Two suspects can each either cooperate (stay silent) or defect (betray). Individually rational defection produces a collectively worse outcome than mutual cooperation. Explains arms races, climate inaction, and competitive price wars.
howToApply: Identify whether your situation is a Prisoner's Dilemma. If yes, look for mechanisms that enable cooperation: reputation, iteration, communication, binding commitments, and enforcement.
whenToUse: Competitive strategy where cooperation would benefit all
Understanding why self-interested behaviour can produce collectively poor outcomes
commonMistakes: Treating all competitive situations as PDs (many aren't)
Ignoring that repeated games allow cooperation to be self-enforcing

name: Paradigm Shifts
origin: Thomas Kuhn · The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
shortDesc: Science advances through anomalies that trigger revolutionary framework changes
fullDesc: Kuhn showed science doesn't advance linearly but through crisis and revolution. Normal science operates within a paradigm; anomalies accumulate until a crisis triggers a wholesale replacement of the framework.
howToApply: Track anomalies in your domain — data that doesn't fit the current model. When anomalies accumulate, consider whether the current paradigm needs partial or wholesale revision.
commonMistakes: Treating all anomalies as requiring paradigm shifts (most are resolved within the current one)
Underestimating social and institutional resistance to paradigm change

name: Cialdini's Six Principles
shortDesc: Reciprocity, Commitment, Social Proof, Authority, Liking, Scarcity
fullDesc: Six principles hardwired into human social psychology that drive compliance. Reciprocity (return favours), Commitment (stay consistent with past choices), Social Proof, Authority, Liking, Scarcity. Both used for persuasion and to defend against manipulation.
howToApply: For ethical persuasion: give first (reciprocity), get small commitments (consistency), show similar users' success (social proof). For defence: when you feel rushed or pulled by one of these, name the principle being used.
commonMistakes: Using them manipulatively rather than to genuinely help customers achieve their goals
Assuming they work equally across all cultures

name: Learned Helplessness
shortDesc: After repeated failure, we stop trying even when success is possible
fullDesc: Dogs given inescapable shocks stopped trying to escape even when escape became possible. Humans generalise repeated failure into global helplessness. Explains why people in poverty, abuse, or chronic failure become passive.
howToApply: For others: create conditions for small, undeniable wins. For yourself: notice global helplessness statements ('I always...', 'I never...') and test whether they're actually true.
whenToUse: Coaching or managing someone who has stopped trying
Recovering from chronic failure or setback
commonMistakes: Mistaking learned helplessness for laziness
Trying to motivate with exhortation before creating conditions for success

name: Spotlight Effect
shortDesc: We overestimate how much others notice our appearance and mistakes
fullDesc: People believe they're being observed and judged more than they actually are. Others are busy in their own mental worlds and notice us far less than we fear. This bias produces excessive self-consciousness and inhibits action.
howToApply: When paralysed by self-consciousness, remember: others are focused on themselves. The audience for your imagined social failure is largely fictional.
whenToUse: Creative or performance contexts where self-consciousness inhibits expression
commonMistakes: Completely ignoring social perception (some attention to it is adaptive)
Using it to dismiss genuine feedback from others

name: Locus of Control
shortDesc: Internal: you control outcomes. External: outcomes are controlled by fate
fullDesc: People with an internal locus believe their actions determine outcomes; external locus people attribute outcomes to luck, fate, or powerful others. Internal locus predicts better academic, career, and health outcomes.
howToApply: Notice your explanatory style after outcomes. If you attribute failure entirely to external forces, test whether internal actions could have changed it. Cultivate agency in controllable domains.
commonMistakes: Assuming internal locus is always better (structural constraints are real)
Conflating internal locus with self-blame

name: Comparative Advantage
origin: David Ricardo · Principles of Political Economy
shortDesc: Trade based on relative, not absolute, efficiency — gains from specialisation
fullDesc: Even if one party is better at everything, both benefit from specialising in what they're relatively better at and trading. Explains why nations trade, why professionals hire assistants, and why teams specialise.
howToApply: Identify what you are relatively best at compared to alternatives. Specialise there. Trade for the rest, even if you could do those things faster than your trading partner.
commonMistakes: Confusing absolute advantage (being best) with comparative advantage (being relatively best)
Ignoring transaction costs that can make self-sufficiency rational despite comparative advantage

name: Prospect Theory
shortDesc: People value gains and losses differently; losses loom larger
fullDesc: Expected utility theory predicts how people should decide; prospect theory describes how they actually do. People are risk-averse for gains and risk-seeking for losses. The value function is steeper for losses than gains.
howToApply: Frame offers as avoiding losses rather than acquiring gains when possible. When you observe irrational risk-seeking, check if someone is trying to recover a loss. Design choices to account for loss aversion.
commonMistakes: Using loss framing manipulatively when the underlying product doesn't deliver value
Treating prospect theory as a universal — cultural variation is significant

name: Mental Accounting
shortDesc: We treat money differently based on its mental category or source
fullDesc: People treat money differently depending on where it came from, what it's earmarked for, or which mental account it belongs to. Casino winnings feel free; salary feels serious. A pound is always a pound — the mental category is fictional.
howToApply: Audit how you treat money from different sources. Check if you spend windfalls or bonuses more freely than earned income. For decision-making, treat all money as fungible.
commonMistakes: Spending 'found money' (tax refunds, bonuses) freely while saving earned income compulsively
Using mental accounts in ways that prevent optimal trade-offs

name: Time Value of Money
shortDesc: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow
fullDesc: Money available now is worth more than the same amount in the future because of its earning potential. The present value of future cash flows must be discounted at an appropriate rate. Underpins all of corporate finance.
howToApply: For any future payment or investment, calculate its present value using an appropriate discount rate. Compare alternatives on a present-value basis, not nominal amounts.
whenToUse: Pricing contracts with future payment streams
commonMistakes: Using too low a discount rate, inflating present value of speculative future returns
Ignoring the time dimension when comparing financial alternatives

name: Situational Leadership
origin: Hersey & Blanchard · Management of Organizational Behavior
shortDesc: Match leadership style to team member's development level
fullDesc: Effective leadership style depends on the follower's competence and commitment. Directing suits beginners; coaching suits competent-but-uncertain people; supporting suits capable-but-unmotivated people; delegating suits high-competence high-commitment individuals.
howToApply: Assess each team member's competence and motivation in their specific role. Apply the matching leadership style. Avoid using one style for everyone.
whenToUse: Diagnosing why a high performer is suddenly struggling
commonMistakes: Using the same style for all (usually either too directive or too hands-off)
Assessing development level globally rather than task-specifically

name: Pyramid Principle
shortDesc: Lead with the conclusion, then support with evidence in logical order
fullDesc: Consulting communication structure: state your conclusion first (the top of the pyramid), then support it with three or so key arguments, each of which is in turn supported by evidence. Respects the reader's time and prevents burying the lead.
howToApply: Write your conclusion first. Identify three supporting arguments. Ensure each argument is distinct, collectively exhaustive, and mutually exclusive (MECE). Support each with data or logic.
whenToUse: Any communication where the audience is time-constrained
commonMistakes: Burying the conclusion at the end after a journey narrative
Treating it as appropriate for all communication (bottom-up narrative is sometimes more persuasive)

name: Lateral Thinking
shortDesc: Approach problems from unexpected angles; escape vertical logic patterns
fullDesc: Vertical thinking deepens existing channels. Lateral thinking cuts across them. Tools include random entry (introduce random stimulus), provocation (state something deliberately wrong to trigger new thinking), and reversal (invert the problem).
