howToApply: When stuck, introduce a random object. Brainstorm connections between it and your problem. Use deliberate provocation: 'What if we charged customers to complain?' Use connections as a springboard to novel ideas.
whenToUse: Finding solutions outside the obvious solution space
commonMistakes: Using it for execution problems where deep vertical thinking is appropriate
Treating lateral thinking outputs as solutions rather than starting points

name: Six Thinking Hats
origin: Edward de Bono · Six Thinking Hats
shortDesc: Six modes of thinking (facts, emotions, risks, benefits, creativity, process)
fullDesc: Each hat represents a thinking mode: White (facts), Red (emotions/intuition), Black (risks/caution), Yellow (benefits/optimism), Green (creativity/alternatives), Blue (process/meta). Groups wear hats sequentially to prevent argument and ensure comprehensive thinking.
howToApply: In group decisions, explicitly rotate through hats. Separate fact-finding from risk assessment from creative generation. The Black hat (risk) is most often skipped; make it mandatory.
whenToUse: Avoiding groupthink by separating thinking modes
commonMistakes: Wearing all hats simultaneously (the point is separation)
Skipping the Black hat because it feels negative

name: Overton Window
shortDesc: The range of politically acceptable ideas shifts over time
fullDesc: At any time, there is a window of ideas deemed acceptable for serious political discussion. Ideas outside the window are 'radical'. The window moves — what was unacceptable becomes policy. Advocates shift the window by making extreme positions mainstream.
howToApply: Identify where an idea sits in the current Overton Window. To shift policy, shift the window first by making more radical versions mainstream. To communicate effectively, calibrate to where the audience's window is.
whenToUse: Understanding why some ideas succeed and others fail politically
commonMistakes: Assuming the window is fixed (it moves in both directions)
Confusing what's politically possible with what's right

name: Hero's Journey
origin: Joseph Campbell · The Hero with a Thousand Faces
shortDesc: Transformation narrative: ordinary world → challenge → ordeal → return
fullDesc: Campbell identified a universal story structure across mythologies: hero leaves ordinary world, crosses threshold, faces trials, confronts ordeal, gains reward, returns transformed. Used in film, branding, and change communication.
howToApply: Structure any transformation story using the stages. Position your audience as the hero, your product/idea as the guide. The ordeal is the transformation — don't skip it.
commonMistakes: Making the brand/company the hero rather than the customer
Treating it as a rigid script rather than a flexible pattern

name: Curse of Knowledge
shortDesc: Experts struggle to explain concepts because they can't imagine not knowing them
fullDesc: Once you know something, you can no longer remember what it was like not to know it. This makes expert-to-novice communication systematically poor. Teachers assume students already have prerequisite knowledge; writers assume readers share their context.
howToApply: Before communicating expertise, identify the minimum prerequisite knowledge your audience has. Explicitly name and fill each gap. Test by explaining to actual novices.
commonMistakes: Asking 'is this clear?' (people with the curse can't judge)
Solving it once and assuming the problem is fixed

name: Double-Loop Learning
shortDesc: Don't just fix mistakes — question the assumptions that caused them
fullDesc: Single-loop learning: detect and correct error within existing norms. Double-loop learning: question whether the norms themselves are correct. Most organisations are good at the former and terrible at the latter.
howToApply: After any significant failure, run two analysis levels. First: what did we do wrong? Second: what assumptions or values led us to act that way? The second is double-loop learning.
commonMistakes: Treating retrospectives as process improvement without examining underlying beliefs
Conflating double-loop learning with blame

name: Red Queen Effect
shortDesc: You must keep running just to stay in the same place
fullDesc: In evolutionary competition, each species must continually adapt just to maintain fitness against co-evolving competitors. Applied to business: markets, technology, and talent require constant improvement just to maintain position.
howToApply: Identify domains where competitive dynamics require continuous investment just to stay level. Separate these from blue ocean spaces where improvement creates durable advantage.
whenToUse: Understanding why industries require constant R&D
commonMistakes: Investing only to keep pace when you should be escaping the treadmill via differentiation
Ignoring Red Queen dynamics in markets that appear stable

name: Punctuated Equilibrium
shortDesc: Evolution proceeds in bursts separated by long stable periods
fullDesc: Against Darwin's gradualism, Gould and Eldredge found the fossil record shows long periods of stability punctuated by rapid change. Applies to markets, organisations, and technology: long plateaus punctuated by disruptive leaps.
howToApply: Identify whether your industry is in a stable period or at a punctuation point. In stable periods, optimise. At punctuation points, be willing to cannibalise your own position to survive the transition.
commonMistakes: Assuming gradual improvement will protect against punctuated disruption
Treating every disruption narrative as a genuine punctuation when most are hype

name: Kotter's 8-Step Change Model
shortDesc: Create urgency → coalition → vision → communicate → empower → wins → consolidate → anchor
fullDesc: Kotter's research on failed change found eight consistent errors. His model addresses each: build urgency, form a guiding coalition, create a vision, communicate it relentlessly, empower action, generate short-term wins, consolidate, and anchor in culture.
howToApply: Before any large change initiative, run through the eight steps as a checklist. Skipping urgency creation is the most common and fatal error.
commonMistakes: Declaring victory too early and losing momentum
Communicating the vision once rather than repetitively

name: Kübler-Ross Change Curve
origin: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross · On Death and Dying
shortDesc: People move through: denial → anger → bargaining → depression → acceptance
fullDesc: Originally described stages of grief, now widely applied to any significant change or loss. People move through stages at different speeds; some get stuck. Understanding stage predicts effective support.
howToApply: When managing change, diagnose which stage individuals are in. Don't try to skip stages. Match your communication to the stage: information helps in denial; empathy helps in depression.
whenToUse: Supporting people through loss or transition
commonMistakes: Treating stages as linear and sequential when people move back and forth
Pushing acceptance before anger and bargaining have been acknowledged

name: Thucydides Trap
shortDesc: When a rising power threatens an established one, war often follows
fullDesc: Named after Thucydides' analysis of Sparta and Athens: when a rising power threatens to displace a ruling one, the resulting fear and structural stress make violent conflict likely. Allison found it occurred in 12 of 16 historical cases.
howToApply: In any competitive or geopolitical analysis involving an incumbent and a fast-growing challenger, explicitly model the incumbent's fear response. Design strategies that reduce threat perception.
whenToUse: Competitive strategy when you're a challenger
commonMistakes: Treating the trap as inevitable — 4 of 16 cases avoided war
Applying it only to nation-states rather than competitive dynamics generally

name: Moral Panics
origin: Stanley Cohen · Folk Devils and Moral Panics
shortDesc: Media-amplified fear about perceived threats to social values
fullDesc: Moral panics involve exaggerated social concern about a group or behaviour portrayed as a threat to social values. Media amplify, experts condemn, and policies overreact. The threat typically subsides, often replaced by another panic.
howToApply: When a social threat narrative intensifies, apply the moral panic checklist: is the threat exaggerated? Is a scapegoat group being constructed? Are moral entrepreneurs benefiting? Are countervailing facts suppressed?
whenToUse: Policy analysis of new social threats
commonMistakes: Dismissing all public concern as moral panic (some threats are real)
Using the framing to shut down legitimate discussion
